content: Pulled elbow, also known as nursemaid's elbow, is a frequent injury in young children. It typically occurs when a sudden pull on the arm, often by an adult or taller individual, causes the radial head to partially dislocate (subluxation) by slipping through the annular ligament. This injury can also result from a fall or twisting motion. Affected children experience sudden, sharp pain and an inability to use the injured arm. The standard treatment involves manual reduction of the subluxed radial head, with the most common techniques being forearm supination combined with flexion or hyperpronation. However, the relative effectiveness of these methods remains uncertain. The objective of this study was to compare the benefits and harms of different manipulative techniques for treating pulled elbow in young children. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that evaluated these interventions. The primary outcome assessed was the failure of the first attempt at reduction, necessitating further treatment. The review included nine trials involving 906 children under the age of seven, with 58% of participants being female. Five of these trials were newly identified in this update. Most studies were conducted in emergency departments or ambulatory care centers, with one study performed in a tertiary pediatric orthopedic unit. Geographically, four trials were conducted in the United States, three in Turkey, one in Iran, and one in Spain. Five trials were at high risk of selection bias due to inadequate allocation concealment, and all trials were at high risk of detection bias because assessors were not blinded. Eight trials compared the hyperpronation method with the supination-flexion method. The evidence, though of low quality, suggested that hyperpronation was more effective, with a lower failure rate on the first attempt (9.2% failure rate for hyperpronation versus 26.4% for supination-flexion). This corresponds to a risk ratio of 0.35 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.25 to 0.50) based on data from 811 participants across eight studies. For every 1,000 children treated with hyperpronation instead of supination-flexion, there were an estimated 174 fewer failures on the first attempt (95% CI 134 to 201 fewer). The number needed to treat (NNT) was calculated to be six (95% CI 5 to 8), meaning that six children would need to be treated with hyperpronation rather than supination-flexion to prevent one additional failure on the first attempt. Evidence regarding pain during or after the manipulation was of very low quality, making it unclear whether there is a difference in pain levels between the two methods. Similarly, very low-quality evidence from six studies suggested that repeat hyperpronation might be more effective than repeat supination-flexion after an initial failure, but this finding is uncertain. Other outcomes, such as adverse effects and recurrence rates, were either not reported or unsuitable for pooling. Ultimate failure rates, which varied due to differences in study protocols, ranged from no failures in two studies to six failures (4.1% of 148 episodes) in one study. One trial compared supination-extension with supination-flexion, but the evidence was of very low quality due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. This trial found no clear difference in failure rates on the first attempt between the two methods. In conclusion, low-quality evidence from eight small trials suggests that the hyperpronation method may be more effective than the supination-flexion method for the initial reduction of pulled elbow in young children. However, for other outcomes, no definitive conclusions can be drawn due to very low-quality evidence or lack of reporting. The authors recommend conducting a high-quality randomized clinical trial to compare hyperpronation and supination-flexion definitively. Before such a trial, a survey among clinicians is suggested to assess the degree of clinical equipoise and to optimize study design and recruitment strategies.
